newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian telecoms seen booming on investment plans.
newsitem.headline: Russian telecoms seen booming on investment plans.

text.p: Russian phone companies, already outperforming other shares, are seeking local and foreign funds to revamp their underdeveloped systems.
As a result, telecoms could be one of the hottest sectors in the expected 1997 Russian equities boom, analysts say.
"Telecoms will be one of the leaders, if not the leader, in Russia for 1997 because of their quest for financial support and their development plans," an analyst at Troika-Dialog said.
Russia has 18 phones per 100 people, according to official statistics, against 56 in the U.S. and 40 in Western Europe.
That points to enormous potential for growth in Russia, where even people who now have phones can still have trouble getting through on local and intercity lines.
Telecoms have already expanded, raising the number of phones per 100 people from 15 in mid-1996, while the economy shrank.
"The telecoms have outpaced everyone so far except maybe the energy sector. But that should change," said Renaissance Capital telecoms analyst Yuri Krapivin.
"Once we see a turnaround in the economy and GDP starts climbing there will be tremendous growth in telecommunications."

In the last three months the Skate Press index of 12 Russian telecoms shares has risen 52 percent while its general 100-share index has risen 42 percent. Over a year the relative performance of telecoms has been even more dramatic.

Several national and regional telecoms companies have announced plans to issue Eurobonds or place shares in foreign markets, and many companies intend to improve cash-flow by charging for local calls, previously free in Russia.

International call server AOOT Mezhdugorodnoi i Mezhdunarodnoi Elektricheskoi Svyazi Rostelekom, like many foreign operators, has cut international charges by about 20 percent in January to stimulate traffic.
Over one third of Russia's 87 regional telecoms concerns plan to charge for local calls to fund growth and close the gap between commercial and residential prices. Some have already started.
AO Tyumentelekom has charged for local calls since 1995.

AO Svyazinform Nizhegorodskaya Oblast in Nizhny Novgorod and AO Uralsvyazinform Permskaya Oblast in Perm have introduced charges for local calls in some areas, but until the entire regions are equipped, it will be difficult to gauge how traffic flows and volumes have changed, analysts said.
Other companies planning to charge locally are Moscow operator MGTS and St Petersburg's PTS which have higher than average phone densities of 45.6 and 37.4 per 100 respectively.
Traffic is unlikely to drop after the first few months once users see that bills have not risen sharply, Krapivin said.

"Charging for local calls will at least give the companies valuable information regarding traffic pressures and patterns, and will allow them to be elastic in setting the rates," said the Troika-Dialog analyst.
Regional telecoms companies are also turning to foreign investors to fund their expansion.
OAO Moskovskaya Gorodskaya Telefonnaya Set (MGTS) has said it will issue Eurobonds in the first half of 1997 to raise about $100m for telecommunications finance development.

Uralsvyazinform plans to issue American Depositary Receipts by the second quarter of 1997. Russian telecoms companies have so far not issued ADRs, but shares of other Russian companies which have done so have tended to outperform the market.
AO Kubanelektrosvyaz has hired a Western auditor, indicating that it too could tap international equity markets.
Rostelekom too is planning a Eurobond, but says it will take another few months to resolve issues holding up its ADRs.
Russia intends to sell 49 percent of Svyazinvest, which holds government stakes in Rostelekom and regional companies.
Of this 25 percent will go to foreign portfolio investors and 24 percent to Russian investors. A deal at the end of 1995 to sell 25 percent to Italy's STET SpA fell through.
